🇮🇳 India is preparing to put corporate bonds onchain

India plans to launch its first tokenised corporate bond issuance in September, according to Reuters.

The pilot will involve state-owned power financier REC and bonds worth less than 5 billion rupees, approximately $57 million.

Blockchain will be used to record:

• issuance
• ownership
• trading
• settlement

Investors will purchase the bonds using India’s wholesale central bank digital currency. They will need both a CBDC wallet and a new digital securities wallet called DEMAT 2.0.

The pilot will initially be available only to selected investors. A secondary market is expected to follow in December.

The important point is that these bonds are not being turned into speculative crypto assets.

They remain regulated debt instruments. Blockchain changes the infrastructure behind them by allowing ownership and settlement to be recorded on the same digital system.

This is where tokenisation becomes practical.

The asset remains familiar.

The process behind it becomes faster and more programmable.

🔗 Source: Reuters⁠

CONFIRMED — JAPAN JUST CROSSED A LINE MEDICINE HAD BEEN APPROACHING FOR 20 YEARS.

On March 6, 2026, Japan granted conditional approval to the world’s first two therapeutic products made from induced pluripotent stem cells.

Not a concept.

Not a computer simulation.

The products have names: AMCHEPRY and RiHEART.

AMCHEPRY begins with donor cells reprogrammed into an earlier, highly versatile state. Scientists then guide them toward becoming the precursors of dopamine-producing neurons—the cells that are progressively lost in Parkinson’s disease—and transplant them into the brain.

RiHEART takes a different path. Heart-muscle cells created from iPS cells are formed into living sheets and placed directly on the surface of a severely damaged heart.

The early human studies were small: seven Parkinson’s patients and eight heart-failure patients. That is exactly why the approvals are conditional and time-limited, with more evidence still required.

But the historical shift is real.

A cell can now be reprogrammed, redirected, manufactured as a medical product—and used in an attempt to restore function inside the human brain or heart.

Is this a mythical cure-all machine? No.

Is it documented regenerative medicine moving from laboratory research toward real clinical use? YES.

Twenty years ago, this sounded like science fiction.

Today, Japan has placed it inside the medical system.
